# **morpheme**

## <span style="color:green"><b>smallest linguistic unit</b></span> <b>with</b> <span style="color:blue"><b>meaning</b></span>


---
## **Homophones and Allomorphs**
<br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid orange; background-color:#FFF176"><h3><span style="color:black;"><b>homophones</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid orange">
    <ul>
      <li>
        sound the same, but mean different things<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li>
            <i>small-er → <span style="color:orange">-er</span></i> = <span style="color:orange">'more'</span>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp
            <i>help-er → <span style="color:orange">-er</span></i> = <span style="color:orange">'agent'</span>
          </li>
          <li>
            <i>paper-s → <span style="color:orange">-s</span></i> = <span style="color:orange">PLURAL</span>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp
            <i>see-s → <span style="color:orange">-s</span></i> = <span style="color:orange">3SG PRESENT</span>
          </li>
        </ul>
      </li><br>
      <li>
        these are <span style="color:orange"><b>different morphemes</b></span> that happen to sound the same
      </li><br>
      <li>
        <span style="color:orange"><b>homophonous</b></span>
      </li>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid blue; background-color:#A4C2F4"><h3><span style="color:black"><b>allomorphs</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid blue">
    <ul>
      <li>
      mean the same thing, but are pronounced differently<br><br>
        <ul class="two-col-grid">
          <li>
            <i>wug<span style="color:blue">-s</span></i>,
            <i>peff<span style="color:blue">-s</span></i>,
            <i>gutch<span style="color:blue">-es</span></i>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp
            <i>talk<span style="color:blue">-ed</span></i>,
            <i>buzz<span style="color:blue">-ed</span></i>,
            <i>land<span style="color:blue">-ed</span></i>
          </li>
          <li>
            <i><span style="color:blue">magic</span>-al</i>,
            <i><span style="color:blue">magic</span>-ian</i>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp
            <i><span style="color:blue">clear</span>-ing</i>,
            <i><span style="color:blue">clar</span>-ify</i>
          </li>
        </ul>
      </li><br>
      <li>
        each of these is a <span style="color:blue"><b>separate morpheme</b></span> with multiple pronunciations and each pronunciation is called an <span style="color:blue"><b>allomorph</b></span> of that morpheme
      </li>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

## **Types of Morphemes I: Free vs. Bound**
<br>
compare two **lexical entries** we have seen:
<br><br>
.pull-left[
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">label</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><span style="color:#CC0033">'dog'</span></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><span style="color:#CC0033">'teach'</span></td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><b>phonological representation</b></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">/dɑg/</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">/tiːtʃ/</td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><b>semantic representation</b></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">{x: x is a <i><b><span style="color:green">dog</span></b></i>}</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">{&lt;x, y&gt;: x <i><b><span style="color:green">teaches</span></b></i> y}</td>
  </tr>
</table>
]

.pull-right[
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse;">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">label</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><span style="color:#CC0033">'-er'</span></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><span style="color:#CC0033">'-able'</span></td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><b>phonological representation</b></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">/ər/</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">/əbəl/</td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;"><b>semantic representation</b></td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">one who does <i><b><span style="color:orange">X</span></b></i> action</td>
    <td style="width:15%; text-align:center; border:1px solid black;">able to be<br><i><b><span style="color:orange">X</span></b></i>-ed</td>
  </tr>
</table>
]
<br>

</div>
]
.pull-right[

  <h2><b>
    <span style="color:green">bound morpheme</span>
  </b></h2>
  cannot stand alone<br>
  e.g. <i>-er</i>, <i>-s</i>, <i>cran-</i>
</div>
]

## **The Same Morphemes Might<br>Behave Differently in Another Language**
<br>
- a **single** morpheme in one language can be translated **into more than one** morpheme (or even multiple words) in another language<br><br>

- just because a morpheme corresponds to a word in English **does NOT mean** it is necessarily a word in the given language<br><br>


.pull-left[
.pull-left[
**Spanish**<b>:</b>
]
.pull-right[
*habl-ar*<br>
*habl-o*<br>
*habl-as*<br>
*habl-ábamo*s<br>
*habl-aríamo*s<br>
*habl-a*<br>
*<i>habl</i>
]
]
.pull-right[
.pull-left[
‘to speak’ (infinitive) <br>
‘I speak’<br>
‘you speak’<br>
‘we were speaking’<br>
‘If we spoke’<br>
‘Speak!’ (imperative)<br>
???
]
.pull-right[

]
]
<br>
- we can easily see that the morpheme ***habl*** corresponds to the English word ***speak***, but it does not correspond to a word in Spanish, ***habl*** must always occur with other morphemes, so in Spanish it is a **bound morpheme**

## **Types of Morpheme II: Root vs. Affixes**
<br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid #CC0033; background-color:#FF8686"><h3><span style="color:black;"><b>root</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid #CC0033">
    <ul>
      <li><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>"base"</b></span> morpheme to which other morphemes are attached</li><br>
      <li>contributes the <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>core meaning</b></span> of the word</li><br>
      <li>if a word has a single morpheme, that morpheme is a root</li><br>
      <li>examples: <i><span style="color:#CC0033">danc</span>-ing</i>, <i>dis-<span style="color:#CC0033">appear</span></i>, <i><span style="color:#CC0033">help</span>-less-ness</i>, <i><span style="color:#CC0033">elephant</span></i></li><br>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid green; background-color:#62D095"><h3><span style="color:black"><b>affix</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid green">
    <ul>
      <li>morpheme that is <span style="color:green"><b>attached to the root</b></span></li><br>
      <li><span style="color:green"><b>prefixes</b></span> go before root, <span style="color:green"><b>suffixes</b></span> go after root – both are affixest</li><br>
      <li>a word can have multiple prefixes or suffixes</li><br>
      <li>examples: <i><span style="color:green">in-</span>complete</i>, <i>act<span style="color:green">-ive</span></i>, <i><span style="color:green">un-</span>trust<span style="color:green">-worthy</span></i>, <i><span style="color:green">will</span>-ing-ly</i></li><br>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

---
## **Types of Morpheme II: Root vs. Affixes**
<br><br><br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid #CC0033; background-color:#FF8686"><h3><span style="color:black;"><b>root</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid #CC0033"><br>
    <ul>
      <li>
        a word with <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>more than one root</b></span> is called a <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>compound</b></span> word:<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li><i>house-cat</i>, <i>ginger-bread</i>, <i>sun-flower</i></li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <br><br>
      <li>
        a word with a single <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>one root</b></span> is called <span style="color:#CC0033"><b>simple</b></span>, even if it has affixes:<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li><i>cat</i>, <i>eat-s</i>, <i>be-friend</i></li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul><br>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

--
<br><br>
### **compound/simple vs. complex/simplex**

---
## **Types of Morpheme II: Root vs. Affixes**
<br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid green; background-color:#62D095"><h3><span style="color:black"><b>affix</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid green">
    <ul>
      <li>most common affixes are <span style="color:green"><b>prefixes</b></span> and <span style="color:green"><b>suffixes</b></span></li><br>
      <li>
      some languages also exhibits <span style="color:green"><b>infixes</b></span>, which go <span style="color:green"><b>INSIDE</b></span> the root:<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li><b>Tagalog</b>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp <i>bili</i> 'buy' → <i>b<span style="color:green">-um-</span>ili</i> 'to buy'</li>
          <li><b>English</b>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp <i>absolutely</i> → <i>abso<span style="color:green">-****-</span>lutely</i></li>
        </ul>
      </li><br>
      <li>
      or <span style="color:green"><b>circumfixes</b></span>, which go <span style="color:green"><b>AROUND</b></span> the root:<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li><b>Indonesian</b>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp <i>ajar</i> 'teach' → <i><span style="color:green">pel-</span>ajar<span style="color:green">-an</span></i> ''lesson/teaching''</li>
          <li><b>English</b>&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp&nbsp <i>bold</i> → <i><span style="color:green">em-</span>bold<span style="color:green">-en</span></i> </li>
        </ul>
      </li><br>
      <li>
      infixes and circumfixes are a bit rare, so if you think you have found one:<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li>for an <span style="color:green"><b>infix</b></span>, check if it is really inside the root but not two pre/suffixes</li>
          <li>for a <span style="color:green"><b>circumfix</b></span>, chech if it is inseparable and means one thing</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

## **Inflectional Morphemes**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0914/inflederi.png" width="55%">
</div>
]

--

.pull-right[
consider these words and affixes on the left: <br><br>
- the **first** affix in each group (marked <span style="color:#cc0033"><b>red</b></span>) doesn’t really change the word’s core meaning – instead, it adds grammatical nuance:<br><br>
  - *violin-s* = *violin* **+ MORE THAN ONE**
  - *agree-d* = *agree* **+ PAST**
  - *larg-er* = *large* **+ MORE**<br><br>
- the process of adding grammatical nuance is called **inflection**, and these affixes are therefore **inflectional morphemes**<br><br>
  - inflecting a verb is <b>conjugating</b>
  - inflecting a noun is <b>declining</b>
]

---
## **Derivational Morphemes**
<br>
.pull-left[
<div style="text-align:center">
<img src="../pic/0914/inflederi.png" width="55%">
</div>
]

--

.pull-right[
consider these words and affixes on the left: <br><br>
- the <span style="color:green"><b>second</b></span> affix in each group (marked <span style="color:green"><b>green</b></span>) changes the word’s meaning substantially, and can even change its <b>part of speech</b> – adding them <b>makes a new word</b><br><br>
  - *violin* (musical instrument, **N**)<br>
    *violin<span style="color:green"><b>ist</b></span>* (a person, <span style="color:green"><b>N</b></span>)<br>
  - *agree* (share opinions, **V**)<br>
    *agree<span style="color:green"><b>ment</b></span>* (contract, <span style="color:green"><b>N</b></span>)<br>
  - *large* (big, **Adj**)<br>
    *<span style="color:green"><b>en</b></span>large* (make big, <span style="color:green"><b>V</b></span>)<br><br>
- the process of forming new words is called <span style="color:green"><b>derivation</b></span>, and these affixes are therefore <span style="color:green"><b>derivational morphemes</b></span>
]

---
## **Types of Morphemes III**
### **Inflectional vs. Derivational**
<br>
<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse">
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid green; background-color:#62D095"><h3><span style="color:black"><b>inflextional</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid green">
    <ul>
      <li><span style="color:green"><b>inflectional morphemes</b></span> are used to <b>inflect</b> words</li><br>
      <li>they add grammatical nuance but do not change the core meaning</li><br>
      <li>in English, they’re mostly used to conjugate verbs (<i>jump</i> → <i>jump<span style="color:green">-ed</span></i>), pluralize nouns (<i>cat</i> → <i>cat<span style="color:green">-s</span></i>), and form the comparative and superlative
of adjectives (<i>bright</i> → <i>bright<span style="color:green">-er</span></i> → <i>bright<span style="color:green">-est</span></i>)</li>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"></td>
    <td style="width:10%; text-align:center; border:3px solid #CC0033; background-color:#FF8686"><h3><span style="color:black;"><b>derivational</b></span></h3></td>
    <td style="width:1%; text-align:center;"><span style="color:white">-</span></td>
    <td style="width:40%; text-align:left; border:3px solid #CC0033">
    <ul>
      <li><span style="color:#CC0033"><b>derivational morphemes</b></span> are used to derive <span style="color:#CC0033">new words</b></span></li><br>
      <li>they change the core meaning of the word in some way</li><br>
      <li>they can, but do not always, change a word's part of speech<br><br>
        <ul>
          <li>
            <i>simple</i> → <i>simpl<span style="color:#CC0033">-ify</span></i>,
            <i>exist</i> → <i>exist<span style="color:#CC0033">-ence</span></i>,
            <i>pack</i> → <i><span style="color:#CC0033">un-</span>pack</i>
          </li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>

##**Summary for Different Morphemes**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
- <b>root</b> (base; **build**, **flower**)<br><br>
- <b>affix</b> (morpheme that attaches to the base)<br><br>
  - <b>prefix</b> (**un**-do)<br><br>
  - <b>suffix</b> (walk-**ed**)<br><br>
  - <b>infix</b> (rare in English)<br><br>
  - <b>circumfix</b> (**em**-bold-**en**)<br><br>
- <b>free vs. bound morpheme</b>
  - can appear as an independent word?
  - **blue**berry vs. **cran**berry<br><br>
]
.pull-right[
- <b>derivational morpheme</b> (piano --> pian-**ist**) 
  - change core meaning even part of speech<br><br>
- <b>inflectional morpheme</b> (jump --> jump-**ed**) 
  - add some grammatical nuance<br><br>
- <b>homophone</b> (fast-**er**, teach-**er**)
  - same sound, different meanings<br><br>
- <b>allomorph</b> (**magic**, **magic**-ian)
  - same meaning, different sounds<br><br>
- <b>simple word vs. compound word</b>
  - one root = simple (inter-**nation**-al)
  - more than one = compound (**sawhorse**)
]

<div style="
  background:#CC0033;

  font-size:48px;

  padding:40px 0;
  width:100%;
  margin:200px auto;
  text-align:center;
">
Morphological Analysis
</div>

---
## **Morphological Analysis**
<br><br>
- **morphological analysis** is a technique for figuring out how the morphology of a language works.<br><br>
- you can use it to learn how the morphology of an unfamiliar language works – as long as you have a set of words with different morphemes and their translations (**glosses**) into English. <br><br>
- **steps**:
  1. identify any **repeated** sequences of sounds in the dataset – they may be a morpheme<br><br>
  2. identify any **repeated** meanings in the English glosses<br><br>
  3. try to match each meaning from <u>step 2</i> with a potential morpheme from <u>step 1</u> 

---
## **Notes for Moprhological Analysis**
<br><br>
.pull-left[
1. try to find two words that differ by just one meaning or morpheme)<br><br>
2. look out for any potential **homophones** or **allomorphs**<br><br>
3. don’t be afraid to **revise your hypotheses** if the data suggests you’re on the wrong track<br><br>
4. **order** of morphemes matters<br><br>
5. **affixes are picky**
]
.pull-right[
<br><img src="../pic/0914/scientific.jpg" width="85%">
]
